question.leadin: Identify some of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
question.text: King Nebuchadnezzar ("NEB-uh-kud-NEZZ-ur") of Chaldea ("cal-DEE-uh") built these structures for his wife Amytis ("AM-uh-tis") of Media. They consisted of terraces and irrigation structures that serviced a variety of luscious trees.
question.clue: According to Strabo, an early version of Archimedes' Screw was built for use at this location.

swap.text: This man conquered several Sumerian city-states in the 24th and 23rd centuries BCE. It was under him that the Akkadian Empire reached its greatest height.
swap.answerHtml: Sargon the Great [or Sargon I, or Sargon of Akkad; prompt on Sargon]
swap.clue: He appointed his daughter Enheduanna high priestess, and his empire reached its greatest expanse under his grandson Naram-sin.

question.leadin: Leonard Woolley unearthed one of these structures constructed of 720,000 mud bricks and dedicated to the Moon Goddess Nanna.
question.text: Name these stepped temples, a "Great" one of which was built in Ur. Stories of the Tower of Babel may have been inspired by one of these buildings which was dedicated to Marduk.
question.clue: Koldewey also found one that he took to be a temple to Marduk, the name of which, Etemenanki, translates as "The Foundation of Heaven and Earth."

swap.text: The Code of Hammurabi was issued from this ancient city on the Euphrates[yoo-FRAY-teez]River.
swap.clue: A ruler of this city, who won the Battle of Carchemish, destroyed the First Temple during a siege of Jerusalem that marked the beginning of a "Captivity" named for this city.

question.leadin: Answer the following about the reign of Tiglath-Pileser III.
question.text: Tiglath-Pileser ruled the "neo-" version of this empire, whose other leaders included Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal.
question.clue: This empire's final defeat came when Harran fell, an act precipitated by the civil war that broke out between Sin-shar-ishkun and Ashur-etel-ilani.

swap.leadin: They were conquered by the Akkadian Empire around 2270 BC but re-emerged centuries later with the Third Dynasty of Ur.
swap.text: Identify this earliest Mesopotamian civilization who introduced irrigation and invented the wheel.
swap.clue: This civilisation was conquered by the Akkadians around 2270 BC, but its language continued in sacral use, written in cuneiform.

question.leadin: Shalmaneser [shall-mah-NEE-ser] III, a king of this empire, defeated Syrian forces at the Battle of Qarqar ["car-car"].
question.text: Name this ancient empire. Ashurbanipul [ah-shur-BAH-nih-pall] and Sinsharushkin [sin-shar-ISH-kun] ruled this empire, which was conquered by the Babylonians in 608 B་C་E.
question.clue: Its army had a special division that was well-versed in sapping and bridge-building techniques, and that division is often referred to as the first military engineers.

swap.leadin: This ruler's grandmother ordered subjects to support him in the Treaty of Naqia-Zakuto.
swap.text: Name this Assyrian king who ordered the destruction of Elam. This ruler's namesake library was constructed in Nineveh.
swap.clue: He had earlier conquered the Elamite capital Susa, and that defeat of the Kushite armies near Memphis allowed him to take the Egyptian capital.

question.leadin: Name some of the users of ceramics in the ancient world.
question.text: This ancient civilization used clay for building, for tablets on which they invented writing in the form of cuneiform, and for pottery, for which they invented the wheel.
question.clue: The last king of the Lagash dynasty, Lugal-Zage-Si was the last king of the ethnicity, conquering Uruk, where he established his capital.

swap.text: This ensi of Umma was the first to unify the city states of Sumer. Sargon conquered Sumer from this ruler,capturing him at the battle of Uruk.

question.leadin: This man married Amytis, the daughter of the Median King, and Saddam Hussein considered himself the reincarnation of this ruler.
question.text: Name this Chaldean emperor whose conquest of Jerusalem is depicted in the Book of Daniel.
question.answerHtml: <u>Nebuchadnezzar</u> II (This is DB, don’t sweat the number here)
question.clue: Evidence for the Biblical actions of this ruler include a ration list found near the Ishtar Gate which mentions a captive king named Jehoiachin.

swap.text: This last king of the Neo-Babylonian empire restored the Great Ziggurat of Ur and conducted archaeological research in the area. This father of Belshazzar was overthrown by Cyrus the Great.
swap.clue: The loss of this king's forces at the Battle of Opis led to his capital city being captured by Cyrus the Great.

question.leadin: It is unclear whether or not one man with this name was related to Tiglath-Pileser II, but he did succeed him eventually.
question.text: Give this name shared between a man who succeeded Shalmaneser V and a more famous ruler who founded the Akkadian Empire, the first centralized and multi-ethnic empire in history.
question.clue: The earliest known author, the priestess Enheduanna, was the daughter of a ruler of this name who legendarily served as a cupbearer to Ur-Zababa.

swap.text: A law-code for this city was written by Urukagina, who was called the "first reformer" for his efforts against corruption and poverty. This city was home to many statues of its king Gudea, as well as the Stele of the Vultures, which details its conflict with neighboring Umma.
swap.clue: This city-state was home to the Ibgal temple complex, adjacent to which is the first known brewery.

question.leadin: Objects such as an axe with a copper and gold handle adorned with a boar attest to the influence of these people's culture in Ugarit.
question.text: Name these people whose namesake language was primarily spoken in the Mitanni kingdom.
question.clue: This ethnic group largely made up the population of the Mitanni Kingdom to the southeast of the Hittite Empire. Kikkuli ("kee-KOO-lee") wrote a horse training manual in this ethnic group's namesake language, which was most closely related to Urartian.

swap.leadin: This ruler is the main character of the Cutha Legend and The Great Revolt, which may have inspired later legends to blame him for Akkad's conquest by the Gutians.
swap.text: Name this ruler of the Akkadian Empire during its territorial peak and the first to proclaim his own divinity. This ruler's namesake "Victory Stele" depicts his victory over the Lullubi people.
swap.clue: This king who ruled during the height of the Akkadian Empire, and erected a notable victory stele boasting of his defeat of the mountain people of Lullubi and depicting himself as a god.

question.leadin: This city was captured by the Gutians, who came out of the Zagros Mountains in 2180 BCE.
question.text: Name this capital city of a namesake dynasty, founded in the twenty-fourth century BCE.
question.clue: Its exact location is unknown, but is believed to be somewhere on the east bank of the Tigris.

swap.text: One of the languages in Darius the Great's Behistun Inscription was the language of these people, based at Susa. Their Old Kingdom was conquered by Shulgi of Ur, although they rebounded under Kutir-Nahhunte I.
swap.clue: Another ruler of this kingdom installed his son Warad-Sin on the throne of Larsa.

question.text: Michael Witzel has argued that the BMAC may have left linguistic traces in Sanskrit, Avestan, and the language of this kingdom. This kingdom's elites spoke an Indo-Iranian language and ruled from the city of Washukanni.

swap.leadin: Daniel Fleming discussed "early collective governance" in this polity, which was mostly comprised of Sim'alite and Yaminite tribal confederations.
swap.text: Name this polity founded in the early Bronze Age, a major rival of Ebla. "Terrestrial" and "celestial" domains are delineated in a painting from this polity showing a ruler's "investiture."
swap.answerHtml: Mari [accept Tell Hariri] (The painting is the investiture of Zimri-Lim.)
swap.clue: While providing terminology for parts of the body, animals, and economic functions, the names of specific people are largely absent from a peace treaty between this city and Ebla.
